transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what’s been getting to me is… I have a hard time just sitting still. I don’t mean to make it sound worse than it is, but it’s like there’s a little motor running under my skin when I’m supposed to stay put—like during staff meetings or briefings at church events.

I’ll start shifting around, or I’ll stand up, or find some reason to go do something. I’m not trying to be difficult or anything… it’s just uncomfortable sitting there too long. Does that make sense?
Have you started or changed the dose of any new medications recently, especially antipsychotics, anti-nausea drugs, or antidepressants, around the time this restlessness began?
I don’t think so, no. I haven’t started anything like that recently—not that I can remember, anyway. No new medicine or dose change around when this started. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Thinking back, did you notice this same kind of restlessness or difficulty sitting still when you were a child or teenager, or is this something that started more recently in adulthood?

Yeah… I guess if I’m being honest, it wasn’t just recent. I remember back in grade school getting in trouble for popping up out of my seat, or talking over the teacher. Sometimes I’d rush ahead before they’d even finished giving the directions.

My mom used to say I was “wound too tight,” even as a kid. I don’t want to make it sound like I was a terrible kid or anything, but… yeah, that same kind of restlessness was there pretty early on.
Besides the restlessness, do you often have trouble staying focused on tasks, following through on details, or find your mind wandering during conversations or work?

Um… I’m not sure I’d say that’s a big problem for me. I mean, everybody’s mind wanders sometimes, right? But I don’t know that I’ve noticed it enough to call it a main issue.

For me it’s more… I know when I’m uncomfortable staying put. But with focus or details, I’d have to think about that more. I don’t want to give you a wrong answer. Does that make sense?

When you feel that restlessness and need to move, is it usually paired with worrying thoughts or a sense of dread about something, or does it happen even when your mind isn't particularly worried about anything?

It’s not usually because I’m worried, I don’t think. I mean, sometimes meetings or church briefings can be boring or a little stressful like anything else, but it’s more like… my body just doesn’t want to stay parked.

Like I’ll be sitting there and it feels almost like there’s a little motor humming under my skin, if that makes sense. I start shifting around, or I’ll stand up, or find some reason to go check on something. I’m not trying to be difficult or anything—it just gets uncomfortable to sit still too long. Is that the kind of difference you’re asking about?
Do you often find yourself interrupting people, blurting out answers before someone finishes a question, or having trouble waiting your turn in conversations or lines?

Yeah… I mean, I try not to be rude about it, but I probably do that more than I should.

Like if my supervisor, or someone from the church staff, starts giving me instructions, I’ll jump in with what I think they’re about to say before they’ve finished. In my head I’m just trying to show I understand, you know? But sometimes I’m wrong, and then they have to stop and correct me.

I don’t mean to cut people off. It just kind of comes out before I’ve fully let them finish. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Would you say these patterns of restlessness and jumping in before others finish have caused real problems for you—like at work, at home, or in your relationships—not just occasional annoyance?

Yeah… I guess if I’m being honest, it has caused some real problems at work. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, because I do try hard and I’m not trying to be disrespectful.

But there have been complaints, or corrections, when I jump in too fast and miss part of what somebody was telling me. During room turnovers or when we’re deciding supplies, it can create friction because I think I know what’s needed and I move ahead, and then it turns out I didn’t hear the whole thing.

My supervisor actually suggested I talk to the employee assistance program. So… yeah, I suppose it’s more than just annoying sometimes. Is that the kind of problem you mean?
Do you notice this same restlessness and jumping in before others finish happening at home or in your personal relationships too, not just at work or church?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I mean… at home I don’t think anyone has really sat me down and said, “You’re doing this,” if that’s what you mean.

I probably do get a little antsy if I’m sitting too long, and I might jump in sometimes when someone’s talking, but I’ve mostly noticed it being a problem at work or in church settings where there are instructions and other people depending on me. At home it feels less formal, so maybe it doesn’t stand out as much.

Does that answer it the way you’re asking?
Even if no one has pointed it out, do you personally notice yourself feeling restless or interrupting people when you're at home or with family and friends, not just at work or church?

Yeah… I think I do, if I’m paying attention to it. I might not call it “restless” exactly, but I don’t really settle very well.

Like after a shift, instead of just sitting down, I’ll end up puttering in the garage or re-sorting tools, or finding some little thing to straighten up. And at work it’s kind of the same—I’m going from mopping to checking trash to straightening chairs, without really stopping much.

I don’t know if that’s what you mean, but yes, it’s not only at work or church. It shows up at home too, just maybe in a way that seems more useful, so I don’t always think of it as a problem.

Aside from the restlessness and interrupting, have you had ongoing problems with things like breaking rules, getting into fights, being defiant toward authority, or other conduct issues at work, school, or in your community?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had corrections at work, like I said, but not for fighting or breaking rules or being defiant on purpose.

I try to be respectful, maybe sometimes I come off too quick or I don’t slow down enough, but I’m not trying to challenge anybody’s authority. I haven’t had trouble with the law or anything like that. At least… nothing I’d think of as conduct problems. Is that what you mean?
Do you often lose track of things like your keys, phone, or paperwork, or find yourself forgetting appointments or tasks you meant to do?

I’m not really sure… I wouldn’t say it’s a big pattern that I’ve noticed. I mean, I might misplace something now and then like anybody does, but I don’t know that I’m always losing keys or forgetting appointments.

With tasks, I try to keep things pretty routine so I don’t drop the ball. If I do forget something, I usually feel bad about it and try to fix it quick. But I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. Is that the kind of thing you’re asking about?

Thinking back to before you were about 12 years old, did this restlessness and impulsiveness already cause you noticeable trouble—like getting in trouble at school or friction with family—or did that start a bit later?

Yeah… I think it was there pretty early, honestly. I don’t want to make it sound like I was a terrible kid or anything, but in grade school I do remember getting in trouble for popping out of my seat or talking when the teacher was still talking.

And I’d rush ahead before the directions were finished sometimes, like I thought I already knew what to do. My mom used to say I was “wound too tight,” even when I was little. So… yes, I guess it did start before 12, at least some of it.

Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or following through on multi-step instructions at work, even when you're not feeling restless—like missing steps or making careless mistakes because you didn't fully process what was asked?

I’m not sure I’d say that happens often, no. At work I’ve kind of learned to stick to a routine, and if someone gives me steps, I usually try to repeat it back or just get started carefully.

I mean, I’m sure I’ve missed a detail here or there, but I don’t know that it’s a big thing for me when I’m not feeling keyed up. I wouldn’t want to overstate it. Maybe if the instructions are long, I might ask again just to make sure I’ve got it right—is that what you mean?

I don’t know if that’s what you mean, but yes, it’s not only at work or church. It shows up at home too, just maybe in a way that seems more useful, so I don’t always think of it as a problem.

inference.note: Cross-setting impairment (work/church/home) confirmed, supporting hyperactive-impulsive symptoms since childhood; inattentive symptoms not clearly endorsed, so predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation (F90.1) remains most likely, with F90.9 retained pending further clarification.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient shows persistent inattentive symptoms (e.g., forgetfulness, losing items, disorganization) needed to confirm a combined attention/activity disturbance versus an unspecified presentation.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the visit today
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a lifelong pattern (onset before age 12) of motor restlessness ('little motor running under my skin'), difficulty remaining seated during meetings, impulsive interrupting/blurting before others finish speaking, and impulsive task-shifting (moving between chores without settling). These hyperactive-impulsive symptoms occur across multiple settings (work, church, and to a lesser but present degree at home) and have caused functional impairment at work (supervisor referral to EAP, repeated corrections, friction with coworkers). Inattentive symptoms (losing items, forgetting appointments, difficulty following multi-step instructions, careless mistakes) were largely denied or minimized, indicating a predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation rather than combined or inattentive-predominant ADHD. No evidence of conduct disorder features (no rule-breaking, fighting, defiance), no medication-induced akathisia (no recent med changes), and no anxiety-driven restlessness (patient denies worry/dread driving the movement), which helps rule out akathisia and generalized anxiety as primary causes. This pattern fits a hyperkinetic/hyperactive-impulsive ADHD presentation.
